title: Regenerate a severely injured spinal cord with functional reconnection

concept.text: The innovation is biological repair that restores useful communication across a severely injured spinal cord. Success would require more than filling a lesion or growing nerve fibers: signals must pass through regenerated or reconstructed pathways and contribute to useful function. A graft that creates a new neural relay across the injury could meet this goal without regenerating every original axon along its original route. Neural stem-cell transplantation is one investigated approach, but the concept is the functional repair capability rather than a particular treatment.

The intended clinical capability extends beyond improvement on one motor task. It would restore meaningful functions after severe injury, including chronic injuries, with the recovered functions determined by which pathways can be repaired. Voluntary movement, sensation and autonomic control are distinct targets; evidence of motor improvement does not establish restoration of the others. Severe chronic human spinal-cord repair remains a target for demonstration in the supplied evidence.

significance.text: Reliable functional reconnection could make persistent loss of communication between brain and body treatable through biological reconstruction. Even incomplete recovery of skilled hand control could have major practical value. The supplied study discusses wheelchair control, typing and independent eating as possible applications of improved motor function; these are potential human benefits, not outcomes demonstrated in its macaque experiments.

Restoration of sensation or bladder, bowel and other autonomic functions would broaden the impact substantially, but each would require successful repair of the relevant circuits. The reported contusion model retained bowel, bladder and autonomic function, and specific sensory outcomes were not systematically evaluated. Consequently, its motor findings cannot establish recovery of those functions.

Conditional synthesis: the revolutionary change would be a dependable capacity to rebuild useful biological communication, rather than an expectation that every injury could be reversed. Outcomes would depend on injury location and extent, surviving neural circuitry, and the condition of peripheral nerves and muscles. Those dependencies are physiological qualifications, not variables resolved by the supplied study. Biological reconnection would therefore need to be assessed alongside rehabilitation and the person's remaining capacity to use the restored signals.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is reliable, safe reconstruction of pathways that actually carry useful signals across a severe spinal injury. Anatomical growth alone is insufficient evidence. In the supplied study, one macaque had a surviving graft that filled the lesion and produced extensive axonal growth but showed no functional recovery. Rehabilitation engagement complicates interpretation of that individual outcome, yet it illustrates why graft survival and axon counts cannot substitute for demonstrated function.

Concrete engineering barriers include accommodating lesion cavities, managing scar tissue at the lesion interface, achieving graft survival and integrating graft-derived pathways with host tissue. The reviewed article documents fibrous septations and collagenous scar in a subacute experimental lesion and describes scar removal during preparation for grafting. These observations establish practical obstacles in that setting; they do not, by themselves, characterize the full biology of chronic human scars or regeneration throughout the adult central nervous system.

A further scientific barrier is determining what produces recovery. New axons and synaptic-marker colocalization suggest anatomical integration, but do not establish physiological transmission, behavioral necessity or the relative contribution of a reconstructed relay. The authors also discuss trophic factors released by grafted cells that could stimulate host circuits below the lesion. Translation requires distinguishing these mechanisms and showing which can deliver durable benefits after severe chronic injury.

Proposed engineering requirements include directing useful connectivity, avoiding connections that worsen function, and maintaining stable benefits without unacceptable pain, spasticity or treatment-related harm. Harmful miswiring remains a concern to investigate rather than a demonstrated finding of the supplied study. Whether a treatment can safely restore several functions in severe chronic human injuries is unresolved.

current_state.text: In a study published on 17 November 2025, Sinopoulou and colleagues reported improved skilled hand performance in rhesus macaques with experimental unilateral cervical spinal-cord injuries after neural stem-cell transplantation. Grafting occurred 2–5 weeks after injury, with approximately four months of functional assessment. This is a primate proof of principle in a subacute experimental setting, rather than a demonstration of treatment for severe chronic human injury.

The hemisection experiment reported statistically significant improvement in skilled use of the affected right hand for small-object retrieval on a Brinkman board. Its grafted and ungrafted groups were randomized. The hemicontusion comparison instead grouped animals by subsequent graft survival, so it should not be interpreted as the same kind of randomized treatment comparison. Small samples, unequal immunosuppression in the hemisection experiment and the graft-survival grouping in the contusion experiment limit causal generalization.

Graft-derived axons extended into host tissue. Colocalization of labeled axon terminals with the synaptic marker synaptophysin provided anatomical evidence of putative synapses. This supports possible graft-to-host integration but does not independently demonstrate effective signal transmission or prove that those connections caused the behavioral improvement. The retransection and optogenetic evidence discussed by the authors concerned earlier rodent studies, not equivalent causal interventions in these macaques.

The demonstrated functional scope was principally skilled hand and forelimb performance. In the contusion model, bowel, bladder and autonomic functions were retained after injury, so their restoration could not be established. Specific sensory outcomes were not systematically evaluated. Neither broad recovery across several impaired systems nor long-term clinical effectiveness in humans follows from these results.

The supplied review assessed an identified, untruncated full-text article, including its methods and figure captions; figure images and linked supplementary videos were not inspected. The interpretation here therefore rests on the reported text and methods, without independent visual confirmation of those materials. The dated publication precedes the review's 1 November 2026 cutoff, but no freshness assessment was supplied. This record establishes what that study reported, not the field's latest status at the cutoff or whether subsequent work changed the outlook.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing demonstration: randomized clinical trials in people with clearly defined severe, chronic spinal-cord injuries should show durable, clinically meaningful recovery of several impaired functions. Independent replication should establish that the benefit is reproducible across treatment teams and appropriate patient groups. Protocols should prospectively define injury severity, chronicity, meaningful improvement and follow-up duration; the supplied materials establish no numerical thresholds or consensus standard for these choices.
completion_criteria.label: Replicated trials demonstrate durable, clinically meaningful recovery of several functions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed mechanistic requirement: converging anatomical, physiological and clinical evidence should show that regenerated or reconstructed biological pathways carry useful signals and materially contribute to recovery. Where feasible and ethical, assessments should distinguish relay-mediated reconnection from effects on spared pathways, trophic support and rehabilitation alone. Imaging or synaptic markers without evidence of useful transmission would not establish the full capability.
completion_criteria.label: Regenerated or reconstructed pathways transmit useful signals materially supporting recovery

completion_criteria.text: Proposed functional and safety assessment should include voluntary motor control, relevant sensory outcomes, bladder and bowel function, pain, spasticity and long-term treatment safety. Rehabilitation should be standardized or explicitly accounted for, and any immunosuppression requirements should be evaluated as part of the treatment's practical burden. Recovery claims should concern functions that were impaired before treatment and should identify which functions remain unchanged.
completion_criteria.label: Previously impaired functions and long-term treatment safety are assessed

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: successful trials should identify the injury locations, severities, chronicity ranges and patient conditions for which benefits have been demonstrated, along with treatment burdens and nonresponse rates. Replication across a defined range would establish demonstrated breadth; finite trials could not establish that all spinal injuries are repairable or that every lost function can be restored.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrated benefit boundaries, treatment burdens and nonresponse rates are reported

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NRL-06, “Replace lost brain tissue while preserving learned function,” shares the challenge of integrating replacement neural tissue into existing circuits. NRL-05 focuses on restoring communication across a spinal lesion, potentially through new relays; NRL-06 additionally requires preservation of learned functions associated with brain tissue. NRL-16, “Biologically repair the injured visual pathway,” overlaps in biological axon repair and useful circuit reconnection, while targeting vision-specific pathways and outcomes.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-07, “A dependable neural communication channel for profound paralysis,” and NRL-17, “A durable bidirectional neural interface for movement and sensation,” share functional goals with spinal-cord repair. A communication channel or neural interface could enable useful control without biologically reconnecting the injured cord. NRL-05 requires useful biological pathways through or around the lesion, although interface technologies could complement rehabilitation or assessment. These remain distinct capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-12, “Durable immune control and functional remyelination in multiple sclerosis,” overlaps in restoring effective neural signaling. Its defining targets are immune control and myelin repair, whereas NRL-05 addresses regeneration or reconstruction across a severe spinal injury. Remyelination alone would not establish that a disrupted pathway had been rebuilt.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-02, “A general predictive theory of neural circuit computation,” could help explain which reconstructed connections support useful function, but a general theory is a different achievement from a successful repair treatment. NRL-10, “Safe, programmable delivery to selected cells throughout the human brain,” shares delivery and cell-targeting challenges; its brain-wide delivery scope differs from transplantation into a spinal lesion. Stem-cell biology, biomaterials, immunology and rehabilitation are additional enabling disciplines rather than separate completion criteria for NRL-05.

change_log.reason: The review identifies relay formation as part of the concept and the study's stated therapeutic aim.

change_log.change: Replaced the broad adult-CNS and chronic-scarring assertions with the documented spinal-lesion barriers and explicitly bounded their scope.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence supports cavities and scar in subacute experimental injuries, but does not establish the original claims across the adult CNS or specifically in chronic human injury.

change_log.change: Retained harmful connectivity as a proposed engineering concern rather than a demonstrated finding.
change_log.reason: The review found insufficient evidence for the original harmful-miswiring assertion; that limitation does not negate the repair concept.

change_log.change: Added the publication date, rhesus-macaque model, unilateral cervical injury scope, 2–5-week treatment timing and approximately four-month functional assessment.
change_log.reason: These details distinguish the demonstrated subacute primate result from the proposed severe chronic human capability.

change_log.change: Distinguished randomized hemisection groups from hemicontusion comparisons based on subsequent graft survival, and included sample-size and immunosuppression limitations.
change_log.reason: The comparison designs support different strengths of causal inference.

change_log.change: Changed definitive synapse-formation language to anatomical evidence of putative synapses inferred from marker colocalization.
change_log.reason: The reviewed methods and captions do not independently establish physiological transmission or behavioral necessity.

change_log.change: Integrated variable recovery despite extensive axonal growth, alternative trophic mechanisms and the distinction between macaque findings and earlier rodent causal experiments.
change_log.reason: These findings explain why anatomical integration alone does not establish the mechanism of functional recovery.

unresolved_issues: The supplied materials do not establish whether regenerated or reconstructed pathways caused the observed macaque recovery, or how much trophic support and spared host circuitry contributed.
Safe, durable restoration of several functions after severe chronic human spinal-cord injury remains unestablished by the supplied study.
The broader adult-CNS regeneration claim, chronic-specific scar barriers and incidence or consequences of harmful miswiring require additional evidence.
Clinical protocols still need operational definitions of severe and chronic injury, meaningful benefit, follow-up duration and rehabilitation exposure.
The supplied review contains no freshness assessment establishing the field's latest status or continued openness at the 1 November 2026 cutoff.
Figure images and linked supplementary videos were not inspected in the supplied review; conclusions about anatomy and behavior rely on the reported text, methods and captions.

brief.title: Restoring communication across a badly injured spinal cord
possible: People with severe spinal injuries could regain useful movement, sensation or bladder and bowel control, including after long-standing injuries. Restored hand control could help someone type, steer a wheelchair or eat independently.
Biological repair would rebuild pathways that carry signals across the injury. A transplant could provide a new relay between surviving nerve cells without recreating every original connection.
why: Persistent loss of communication between brain and body would become treatable through biological repair. Recovering even part of a lost function could make daily life more independent.

sources.who: Eleni Sinopoulou, Ephron S. Rosenzweig and colleagues
sources.showed: In small macaque experiments, transplants of immature cells that can become nerve cells improved skilled hand performance after recent neck injuries. Nerve fibers grew from the transplants into surrounding tissue.
sources.cited_for: The study supports improved hand function after cell transplantation in primates.
sources.not_established: It did not prove that new connections caused recovery or demonstrate repair of long-standing human injuries.

sources.showed: A trial at a single hospital followed four people with long-standing spinal injuries after cell transplantation. Some showed lasting improvements in movement and sensation scores, but there was no control group.
sources.quote: All subjects tolerated the procedure well with no serious adverse events (SAEs) in the immediate post-procedure period.
sources.cited_for: The trial provides early human findings on treatment tolerability and lasting neurological changes.
sources.not_established: The small trial without a control group cannot establish treatment effectiveness or dependable safety.

sources.who: Maria Teresa Dell’Anno, Xingxing Wang, Marco Onorati and colleagues
sources.showed: In mice, transplanted human cells formed connections and grew axons, the long fibers of nerve cells. Temporarily switching off transplanted nerve cells reduced recovered movement, supporting their role as a relay.
sources.quote: Extensive elongation of both graft and host axons occurs.
sources.cited_for: The experiments support a causal role for transplanted nerve cells in recovered movement in mice.
sources.not_established: They do not establish useful relay-based repair in people with severe, long-standing injuries.

sources.showed: Cell transplants partly restored cardiovascular control in rats with completely severed spinal cords. Cutting the cord again above the transplant erased gains in resting circulation and reflex responses.
sources.quote: Subsequent spinal cord retransection above the graft abolished the recovery of basal hemodynamics and reflexic response.
sources.cited_for: The study supports biological reconnection contributing to recovery of automatic cardiovascular control in rats.
sources.not_established: It does not establish restoration of bladder, bowel or cardiovascular control in humans.

shown: Sinopoulou and colleagues improved skilled hand use in macaques treated soon after experimental neck injuries. New nerve fibers grew into surrounding tissue, but the experiments did not prove that these connections carried the signals responsible for recovery.

Martin and colleagues reported lasting movement and sensation score improvements in some participants in a small human trial without a control group. These findings do not yet establish reliable functional reconnection after severe, long-standing injury.
missing: Reliable repair still needs to overcome injury cavities and scar tissue while keeping transplanted cells alive and connected.
Replicated human trials have yet to establish lasting, meaningful recovery across several previously impaired functions.
Long-term safety remains unresolved, including whether new connections could worsen pain or muscle stiffness.

milestones.label: Replicated trials show lasting recovery of several functions
milestones.explanation: Randomized trials in people with severe, long-standing injuries would have to show meaningful, lasting recovery of several impaired functions, reproduced by independent teams. This would establish dependable benefit.

milestones.label: Rebuilt pathways carry signals that contribute to recovery
milestones.explanation: Anatomy, signal measurements and clinical results would have to show that rebuilt pathways carry useful signals and materially support recovery. This would establish functional reconnection.

milestones.label: Lost functions and lasting treatment safety are assessed
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to assess movement, sensation, bladder and bowel control, pain, stiffness and lasting safety, accounting for rehabilitation and drugs that suppress immunity. This would clarify recovery, harms and treatment burden.

milestones.label: Benefit boundaries, treatment burdens and nonresponse rates are reported
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to identify which injuries and patient conditions benefit, treatment burdens and how often treatment fails. This would define the demonstrated reach of repair.

uncertain: How much recovery comes from new relays, support for surviving nerve cells or rehabilitation remains unresolved.
Trials still need clear definitions of severe and long-standing injury, meaningful improvement and sufficient follow-up.

page.title: Functional reconnection after spinal cord injury
page.definition: Regrown axons—the signal-carrying fibres of nerve cells—or a graft-derived neuronal relay restore communication across an injured spinal cord and recover lost function. The clinical target includes motor-complete injuries, grades A or B on the American Spinal Injury Association Impairment Scale (AIS), at least one year after injury.

goal.need: WHO estimates that 15.4 million people were living with spinal cord injury in 2021, including traumatic and non-traumatic cases. Resulting losses can affect walking, hand use and bowel or bladder emptying.

statements.quote: Researchers are pursuing new methods to repair damage to the spinal cord and restore function after SCI.
Adoption of validated rehabilitation and regenerative therapies into the standard of care that meaningfully improve function, independence and quality of life after SCI.
statements.context: The programme's long-term goal under Rehabilitation and Regeneration.

completion.title: Biological pathways reconstructed across a spinal injury restore function in a confirmatory human trial.
completion.criterion: A confirmatory controlled human trial demonstrates a statistically significant, protocol-defined clinically meaningful functional benefit in a specified population with traumatic, motor-complete injury (AIS A or B) at least one year after injury. Benefit persists for at least one year after treatment, with an acceptable adverse-event profile. Convergent anatomical and physiological evidence establishes that reconstructed biological pathways across the lesion transmit signals contributing to the recovered function. Achievement applies only to the injury level, population and function demonstrated.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; no external criterion combining clinical functional recovery with demonstrated biological reconnection was located.
completion.basis: Searches of ICCP guidelines, MHLW/PMDA cell-product guidance, NIH/SCIRP targets, trial registries and prize criteria found no complete test for human biological reconnection. ICCP supplies the confirmatory efficacy standard and at least one year of follow-up; NSI-566 supplies a chronic-injury eligibility precedent. Attribution of recovered function to reconstructed pathways is the Atlas capability definition, rather than a regulator's approval criterion.

milestones.title: A biological repair candidate restores impaired function in an animal model of spinal cord injury.
milestones.criterion: An injury-matched animal model demonstrates the candidate's intended function, persistence of action and feasibility of clinical benefit. On 23 October 2013, a rat study reported loss of graft-associated cardiovascular recovery after retransection in 5 animals with complete T4 injury. On 17 November 2025, 4 grafted versus 4 control macaques with C7 hemisection achieved 53.4% versus 5.8% final fine-object retrieval after 16 weeks of testing. Both experiments used transplantation 2 weeks after injury; the primate experiment did not establish causal relay transmission.
milestones.set_by: Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, evaluation guidance, section 4(6)[2]. Written for allogeneic iPS-derived cell products for subacute spinal cord injury; it specifies no universal effect size or observation duration.
milestones.threshold_quote: Expression of the function, durability of the action, and feasibility of clinical effects

milestones.title: An animal proof of principle is reproduced across laboratories or animal models.
milestones.criterion: The candidate's proof of principle is reproduced independently in multiple laboratories and/or in more than one type of animal model. A FORE-SCI replication used 20 grafted and 9 control rats with complete T3 transection. It reproduced graft-derived axon outgrowth but found no statistically significant improvement in hindlimb locomotor recovery. Anatomical replication therefore did not reproduce the claimed functional result.
milestones.set_by: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, FORE-SCI replication notice NOT-NS-08-003, released on 16 October 2007.
milestones.threshold_quote: proof of principle experiments should be replicated independently in multiple laboratories and/or in more than one type of animal model.

milestones.title: People with severe chronic spinal injuries receive biological repair in an authorised phase 1 study.
milestones.criterion: First human administration occurs in an authorised phase 1 study following preclinical safety evaluation. NCT01772810 treated 4 people with thoracic AIS-A injury, followed for 42–60 months, and 3 with C5–C7 AIS-A injury, followed for 54–60 months. Both cohorts were uncontrolled. The thoracic report found neurological score changes without functional improvement; the cervical report described exploratory changes confounded by rehabilitation. These findings do not establish clinical efficacy.
milestones.set_by: International Campaign for Cures of Spinal Cord Injury Paralysis clinical guidelines panel, clinical trial design guidance, Phase 1 section.
milestones.threshold_quote: first administration of the therapeutic intervention

milestones.title: A controlled phase 2 study demonstrates therapeutic activity from biological spinal cord repair.
milestones.criterion: A controlled phase 2 study demonstrates a positive change in relevant outcome variables with blinded assessment and a protocol-defined efficacy threshold. ICCP specifies no universal numeric score gain. HuCNS-SC study NCT02163876 enrolled 6 dose-escalation recipients, 6 further recipients and 4 untreated controls with C5–C7 injury 4–24 months earlier. Reported gains fell below the sponsor's efficacy threshold, resulting in early termination.
milestones.set_by: International Campaign for Cures of Spinal Cord Injury Paralysis clinical guidelines panel, clinical trial design guidance, Phase 2 section.
milestones.threshold_quote: positive change in relevant outcome variables

milestones.title: A multicentre trial confirms functional benefit lasting one year after biological spinal cord repair.
milestones.criterion: A phase 3 trial, ordinarily randomised and controlled, confirms the preliminary therapeutic effect as a statistically significant clinical benefit across multiple centres, with an acceptable adverse-event profile. Its primary outcome must capture a change meaningful to the participant's function. A claim of lasting neurological benefit requires follow-up extending to at least one year. Effect size, sample size and statistical thresholds are determined by the specific protocol; ICCP provides no universal numerical values.
milestones.set_by: International Campaign for Cures of Spinal Cord Injury Paralysis clinical guidelines panel, clinical trial design guidance, Phase 3, Outcome Measures and Summary sections.
milestones.threshold_quote: follow-up data extending to at least 1 year.

not_found: No confirmatory clinical result meeting the completion test was identified for cervical or thoracic injury.
No independent replication of the 2025 H9-scNSC macaque functional result was identified.
No controlled efficacy result establishing biological reconnection in severe chronic thoracic injury was identified.
The supplied Dell’Anno et al. Nature PDF and its Nature, PMC and Europe PMC full-text versions could not be opened.
The 2005 Recommended guidelines for studies of human subjects with spinal cord injury could not be opened.
